subject: dbms
title: Unit 3 — Textbook Exercises (Elmasri/Navathe Ch14–15, Silberschatz Ch7)

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 14.6)** Why can we NOT infer a functional dependency automatically from a particular relation state?
options: Because relation states have no data
Because a state satisfying X→Y doesn't guarantee it holds in all legal states — a state can only rule an FD OUT, not prove it
items.explain: An FD is a semantic constraint on every legal state. One state happening to satisfy X→Y is not proof; but a counterexample (equal X, differing Y) disproves it.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 14.2)** The three update anomalies that motivate normalization are:
items.explain: Redundant storage causes insertion (can't add without unrelated data), deletion (lose data when removing a row), and modification (must update many copies) anomalies.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 14.22 / Silberschatz, Ex. 7.36)** Prove or state: any relation schema with exactly two attributes is:
options: Always in BCNF, regardless of its functional dependencies
items.explain: With two attributes, any nontrivial FD must have a determinant that is a superkey (it determines the only other attribute), so a 2-attribute relation is always in BCNF.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 14.24)** For R={A,...,J} with F={AB→C, A→DE, B→F, F→GH, D→IJ}, what is the key of R?
items.explain: A and B are essential (never on a RHS). AB⁺ = {A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J} = R via AB→C, A→DE, B→F, F→GH, D→IJ. So AB is the candidate key.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 14.27)** For R(A,B,C,D,E) with AB→C, CD→E, DE→B, is AB a candidate key? Is ABD?
options: AB is not a key (AB⁺={A,B,C}); ABD is a key (ABD⁺=R, and minimal)
items.explain: AB⁺={A,B,C}≠R, so AB is not a key. ABD⁺={A,B,D,C,E}=R; removing any of A,B,D fails, so ABD is a (minimal) candidate key.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 14.30)** CAR_SALE(Car#, Date_sold, Salesperson#, Commission%, Discount_amt) with PK {Car#, Salesperson#}, Date_sold→Discount_amt, Salesperson#→Commission%. Its highest normal form is:
options: Only 1NF — Salesperson#→Commission% is a partial dependency violating 2NF
items.explain: Salesperson# is part of the key and determines the non-prime Commission% — a partial dependency, so the relation violates 2NF and is only in 1NF.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 14.18)** Why do practical database designs typically aim for BCNF and not higher normal forms?
options: 4NF/5NF dependencies (MVDs, JDs) are hard to detect, and BCNF already removes FD-based redundancy
items.explain: BCNF eliminates all FD-based redundancy; MVDs and especially join dependencies are difficult to detect in practice, so 4NF is rare and 5NF mostly theoretical.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 14.35)** BOOK(Book, Author, Edition, Year) with the MVD {Book} ↠ {Author} | {Edition, Year} should be decomposed (for 4NF) into:
options: Two relations: (Book, Author) and (Book, Edition, Year)
items.explain: The MVD says authors are independent of editions/years for a book. 4NF decomposition splits on the MVD into (Book, Author) and (Book, Edition, Year).

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 15.1–15.2)** What does it mean that Armstrong's inference rules are sound and complete?
options: Sound = they infer only FDs that truly hold; complete = they can infer every FD that holds
They only work on candidate keys
items.explain: Soundness guarantees correctness (no false FDs); completeness guarantees they generate all of F⁺. Together they make IR1–IR3 a complete proof system for FDs.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 15.5)** Does every set of dependencies have a minimal equivalent set, and is it unique?
options: Yes a minimal set exists, but it is NOT necessarily unique
items.explain: Every FD set has at least one minimal (canonical) cover, but different reduction orders can yield different equivalent minimal covers — so it is not unique.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 15.9 & Review 15.11)** A dependency-preserving decomposition of a non-BCNF relation:
options: Cannot be guaranteed to yield BCNF — sometimes BCNF and dependency preservation are incompatible
items.explain: Some relations (e.g. with X→A where A is prime) cannot be decomposed into BCNF while preserving all dependencies — a known limitation; losslessness, not dependency preservation, is the must-have.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 15.11)** Between the dependency-preservation and lossless-join properties, which must DEFINITELY be satisfied?
items.explain: Losslessness is non-negotiable — a lossy decomposition cannot reconstruct the original data. Dependency preservation is desirable but may be sacrificed (e.g. for BCNF).

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 15.21)** REFRIG(M,Y,P,MP,C) with F={M→MP, MY→P, MP→C}. Candidate key = MY. Is REFRIG in 3NF/BCNF?
options: Not in 3NF or BCNF — MP→C has a non-superkey determinant and C is non-prime (transitive)
items.explain: CK is MY. M→MP (M not a superkey) and MP→C (MP not a superkey, C non-prime — transitive). The MP→C transitive dependency violates 3NF (and BCNF).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 7.1)** Decomposing R(A,B,C,D,E) into (A,B,C) and (A,D,E) with F={A→BC, CD→E, B→D, E→A} is lossless because the shared attribute A satisfies:
options: A⁺ = R, so A is a key determining (A,D,E) (and (A,B,C)) — the NJB test passes
A appears in both relations only by accident
items.explain: Shared = A. A⁺ = {A,B,C,D,E} = R (A→BC, B→D, CD→E), so A is a key; (R1∩R2)=A determines all of R2, satisfying the NJB lossless test.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 7.6)** For R(A,B,C,D,E) with F={A→BC, CD→E, B→D, E→A}, the candidate keys include:
options: A, E, BC, and CD (each closure = R)
items.explain: A⁺=R (A→BC→D→E). E→A so E⁺=R. BC⁺: B→D, CD→E, E→A → R. CD⁺: CD→E→A→BC → R. So A, E, BC, CD are all candidate keys.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.24)** Why are certain functional dependencies called 'trivial'?
options: Because they hold in every relation — the RHS is a subset of the LHS (Y ⊆ X)
items.explain: A trivial FD X→Y has Y ⊆ X; it is satisfied by every possible relation (follows from the reflexive axiom) and conveys no real constraint.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.30)** For R(A,B,C,D,E,G) with F={A→BCD, BC→DE, B→D, D→A}, prove AG is a superkey by closure:
options: AG⁺ = {A,B,C,D,E,G} = R, so AG is a superkey
AG is a candidate key but not a superkey
items.explain: AG⁺: A→BCD gives {A,B,C,D,G}; BC→DE adds E → {A,B,C,D,E,G} = R. Since AG determines all attributes, AG is a superkey.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.19)** To show every 3NF schema is also in 2NF, the key observation is:
options: Every partial dependency is a kind of transitive dependency, which 3NF already forbids
items.explain: A partial dependency (non-prime on part of a key) is a special transitive dependency; since 3NF forbids transitive dependencies on the key, any 3NF relation has no partial dependencies, hence is in 2NF.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.40)** Given r(A,B,C,D), does the MVD A ↠ BC logically imply A ↠ B and A ↠ C?
options: Yes, always (like the FD decomposition rule)
No — the FD decomposition rule does not carry over to MVDs in general
Only if A is a key
items.explain: Unlike FDs, an MVD A↠BC does NOT decompose into A↠B and A↠C in general. MVD inference has its own rules; a counterexample relation shows the implication fails.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.41)** Why is 4NF considered more desirable than BCNF?
options: 4NF additionally eliminates redundancy caused by multivalued dependencies, which BCNF (an FD-only condition) ignores
items.explain: BCNF only addresses FD-based redundancy. 4NF further removes the redundancy from nontrivial multivalued dependencies, so it yields a cleaner schema when MVDs are present.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.37)** The three design goals for a relational schema are:
options: BCNF (no redundancy/anomalies), lossless join, and dependency preservation
items.explain: The three goals: a normal form like BCNF (eliminate redundancy/anomalies), the lossless-join property (no spurious tuples), and dependency preservation (constraints enforceable per relation).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.14)** Using F = {X→YZ, Y→XZ, Z→XY}, what does this set demonstrate about canonical covers?
options: A canonical cover is always unique
There can be MORE THAN ONE canonical cover for a given set of dependencies
items.explain: This symmetric set yields several distinct canonical covers depending on which extraneous attributes are removed first — proving the canonical cover is not unique.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ex. 14.29)** Joining ORDER(O#, Odate, Cust#, Total_amount) and ORDER_ITEM(O#, I#, ...) gives RES with key {O#, I#}. Since Odate, Cust#, Total_amount depend only on O#, RES is:
options: Not in 2NF — those attributes are partially dependent on the key {O#, I#} (only on O#)
items.explain: In the joined relation the key is {O#, I#}, but Odate/Cust#/Total_amount depend on O# alone — a partial dependency, so RES violates 2NF (motivating why the natural join was a bad design).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.4)** Using Armstrong's axioms, the union rule (X→Y and X→Z ⟹ X→YZ) is proven by:
options: Augment X→Y by X to get X→XY, augment X→Z by Y to get XY→YZ, then transitivity ⟹ X→YZ
items.explain: Soundness of union: X→XY (augment X→Y by X), XY→YZ (augment X→Z by Y), then X→XY→YZ by transitivity gives X→YZ — derived purely from IR1–IR3.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Review 15.4)** Two sets of functional dependencies are equivalent when:
options: Each set covers the other (E covers F and F covers E), i.e. E⁺ = F⁺
One is a minimal cover of the other
items.explain: Equivalence is mutual cover: every FD of E is inferable from F and vice versa, so their closures are equal. Determined by computing closures both ways.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 7.31)** In R(A,B,C,D,E,G) the dependency AB→CD shows R is not in BCNF when:
options: AB is NOT a superkey of R (yet it determines CD), so the BCNF decomposition algorithm is applied starting from AB→CD
items.explain: If AB→CD holds but AB is not a superkey, BCNF is violated. The BCNF algorithm decomposes R using this FD into (A,B,C,D) and (A,B,...rest), repeating until all pieces are BCNF.
